newsitem.title: UK: China dips toe into physical raw sugar market.
newsitem.headline: China dips toe into physical raw sugar market.

text.p: China is testing the waters of the world sugar market by buying cargoes of raws on an FOB basis before its main importing spree expected some time next year, physical sugar brokers said on Thursday.

The lack of government import licences and the fortunes of domestic and world prices are likely to be determining factors in timing China's buying requirements, which could total up to two million tonnes -- though the exact amount is unclear.
"You've only got two main buyers in China, they haven't got the import licences yet, they have been dipping around with FOB but it's not greatly interesting business," said one broker.
"It's FOB because if they go wrong and they don't get the licences they can simply sell it out as FOBs to someone else."
Another market source said if world raws prices were to fall and China found itself with long futures positions on a FOB basis, it would probably just ship the sugar elsewhere.

The main origin which the Chinese are said to be looking at is Thailand, for geographical reasons if nothing else, but low Thai premiums made it unlikely that any firm C & F business had been concluded as Thailand would be reluctant to sell, he added.
Thai premiums were recently quoted at 60/70 points over New York's March contract for March/May delivery and 85 points for January/March. Premiums for both periods were slightly lower.
But the lower levels still made the market attractive to the Chinese, even though their buying intentions are unclear.

"They're concentrating on Thais -- now that the premium for Thais has come down to a level which saves them some money on freight, it's not cheaper to bring in Brazils or Guatemalans," said a physical sugar trader.
"They can afford to play around a bit...they're not putting in C & F contracts, so we can't actually say that any of the sugar will end up in China yet," he said.
China also imports raw sugar for tolling purposes, when the level of the white/raw premium takes on a key importance.
Other major factors are the actual level of sugar stocks within China and the internal price.

Experts have said that China's firmer domestic sugar price could be a sign that stocks have started to fall. Trade sources said up to two million tonnes of processed sugar are in reserve after massive 1995 imports which have yet to be fully absorbed.
The exact level of stocks is unknown -- and is the subject of much debate -- although they are slowly being eaten through.
"We think their stocks are pretty low...the domestic price has picked up a bit," the trader said.
"I have no doubts at all that they will have to import for the first half or possibly even first quarter because stocks are being used slightly faster than they had expected," he added.
China's internal price for processed sugar stands at over 4,000 yuan a tonne, up from 3,500 at one point recently.
This year for the first time, China ordered sugar mills in major production areas to reserve 300,000 tonnes of sugar at 4,000 yuan a tonne to boost slumping prices.
"It's probably not high enough yet, I think it's got to go above 5,000 before they really feel they have to do something."
"It did pick up towards the Moon Festival and then it slid off a little bit," said one market soource.
China's Moon Festival in September is a four-day celebration when families gather amid colourful lanterns and stay up to watch the moon.
"They always have a flurry of buying before the festival," he said, adding that it was a time of high consumption.
Market sources suggested China could be looking at Australia and Brazil to supply its raw sugar, or possibly Cuba, but this would depend on the two nations' bilateral agreement.
Whenever and from whom China does eventually buy sugar will depend on a decision from the state planning committee in the absence of private buyers.
"I can't see that China can avoid making big decisions on where they see their future imports," the broker said.
"It is a growing consumption area and they will always be in the market." --London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
